paragraphs: Recommendation platforms influence what creators produce by deciding which content receives attention and rewards. This paper studies what happens when creators coordinate as a group to maximize their combined benefit. Its game-theoretic analysis finds that small groups have limited effects on equilibrium, while large groups can substantially change content distribution and user welfare.

The reward mechanism matters. In a system recommending the top K items and rewarding exposure, group strategies can cause substantial welfare losses. Increasing K or introducing more random matching does not necessarily improve welfare. The authors also analyze the Price of Anarchy, a measure of how unfavorable strategic outcomes can be relative to the best outcome, and show that it can become arbitrarily large under exposure rewards.

Rewarding user engagement instead provides stronger guarantees in the studied framework: the Price of Anarchy is at most K + 1 generally and at most 2 in the binary case. Simulations support this mechanism. The findings show why accounting for coordinated creators can materially change conclusions about platform incentives.
icml-2025-beyond-self-interest-how-group.tldr: Coordinated creator groups can harm user welfare under exposure rewards, while engagement rewards provide stronger theoretical welfare guarantees.

paragraphs: Brain graph models can struggle when data from different collection sites or individuals follow different distributions. CIA-GCL addresses this problem by learning which parts of a brain graph contain label-related information that remains stable across these differences. The aim is to support disease classification without relying as heavily on patterns that change between datasets.

The method first constructs a brain graph with node features derived from its topology. It then uses causal decoupling and invariant learning to identify a learnable subgraph intended to retain as much stable, label-related information as possible. This subgraph guides the creation of augmented examples for contrastive learning, connecting the choice of training variations to the information the model should preserve.

The same extracted subgraph is used for classification and highlights local structures relevant to the model's predictions. Experiments on three real-world brain disease datasets report state-of-the-art performance and generalization across sites. The highlighted structures also provide some interpretability, making the method's contribution both improved robustness to distribution shifts and a more inspectable basis for classification.
icml-2025-causal-invariance-aware-augmen.tldr: CIA-GCL builds graph augmentations around learned invariant brain subgraphs to improve disease classification across differing data distributions.

paragraphs: Hierarchical semi-implicit models build expressive probability distributions by stacking multiple layers. They can also accelerate diffusion models when pretrained score networks are available. Their sequential training, however, often converges slowly. CoSIM revisits this layered construction by extending it into a continuous framework, aiming to make training more efficient while retaining its usefulness for generative modeling.

The central component is a continuous transition kernel, which describes how the model moves between states. This enables simulation-free training. The paper also shows consistency when the transition kernel is carefully designed, so that guarantee depends on the chosen construction. Together, these elements provide an approach to multistep distillation that works at the level of probability distributions.

In image-generation experiments, CoSIM matches or exceeds existing methods for accelerating diffusion models and performs better on FD-DINOv2. The contribution connects a change in mathematical representation with a practical training advantage: replacing a sequential hierarchy with continuous transitions supports efficient learning and competitive accelerated generation.
icml-2025-continuous-semi-implicit-model.tldr: CoSIM uses continuous transitions for simulation-free training and competitive multistep distillation of generative models.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering groups data using several representations, or views, of the same underlying items. Most deep approaches assume every view is already available. Deep Streaming View Clustering addresses the setting where new views arrive over time and differ in quality or distribution. Such changes create concept drift, making it harder to maintain a useful clustering structure.

DSVC combines a knowledge base with three learning modules. The first extracts representative features and prototype knowledge from an incoming view. The second aligns those prototypes with the historical knowledge distribution to reduce the impact of drift. The third uses prototype knowledge to guide the data distribution and strengthen the resulting clusters.

After processing a view, DSVC updates its knowledge base so that subsequent views can benefit from what it has learned. This creates an ongoing connection between new observations and accumulated knowledge. Experiments report better clustering performance than 12 state-of-the-art deep multi-view methods operating under static frameworks, even though DSVC handles a dynamic environment. The findings support explicitly managing changes between incoming views.
icml-2025-deep-streaming-view-clustering.tldr: DSVC maintains and aligns prototype knowledge to improve clustering when new data views arrive with changing distributions.

paragraphs: Density ratio estimation asks how strongly two probability distributions differ at a given point. In high dimensions, one approach connects the distributions through a sequence of intermediate distributions and integrates a quantity called the time score along that path. The practical challenge is learning this score from samples accurately and without excessive computation.

This paper introduces a framework that estimates the time score using a conditioning variable. Choosing that variable appropriately makes it possible to write the training objective in closed form. The choice of conditioning therefore has a concrete computational role: it changes how the score-learning problem can be expressed and optimized.

On challenging tasks, the proposed approach learns the time score faster than previous methods and produces density ratio estimates with competitive or better accuracy. The authors also establish theoretical guarantees on estimation error. The contribution combines an easier-to-handle objective with evidence about the resulting estimates, rather than treating faster score learning as sufficient evidence of accurate density ratios.
icml-2025-density-ratio-estimation-with-.tldr: A carefully chosen conditioning variable enables a closed-form objective for faster time-score learning and accurate density ratio estimation.

paragraphs: This paper studies function estimation when data are spread across terminals that can communicate only a limited amount. Each terminal holds multiple independent, identically distributed samples. Under specified regularity assumptions, the authors characterize the best possible worst-case estimation rates across the full range from few samples per terminal to many.

The analysis identifies phase transitions: the form of the optimal rate changes as the number of samples at each terminal increases. This connects regimes that earlier work had treated only at the extremes, with either one sample or dense local samples. It clarifies how local data availability interacts with communication limits in determining achievable statistical accuracy.

To reach these rates, the authors construct a layered estimation protocol using components from parametric density estimation. They prove optimality through information-theoretic arguments, strong data processing inequalities, and the balls-and-bins model. The results also yield rates for density estimation and Gaussian, binary, Poisson, and heteroskedastic regression. The contribution is therefore both a matching protocol and a characterization of the limits it attains.
icml-2025-distributed-nonparametric-esti.tldr: Under regularity assumptions, the paper establishes optimal communication-constrained estimation rates across sparse and dense local sample regimes.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer potential energy savings on neuromorphic hardware, but their accuracy and deployment flexibility remain challenges. In particular, a network trained for a fixed number of inference timesteps may need retraining when that number changes. This paper develops a distillation framework intended to make deep spiking networks effective across the full range of timesteps.

The approach accounts for the networks' spatial and temporal properties and uses logit-based knowledge distillation. Its central objective is to train the implicit models associated with different timestep choices together, enabling deployment adjustments without separate retraining. The authors provide theoretical analysis and empirical evidence supporting convergence of these implicit models across the timestep range.

Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CIFAR10-DVS, and ImageNet report state-of-the-art performance among distillation-based training methods for spiking networks. The practical significance is the combination of accuracy and flexibility: one training framework supports different inference durations. This addresses the deployment constraint directly, alongside the broader effort to make spiking networks more competitive with conventional neural networks.
icml-2025-efficient-logit-based-knowledg.tldr: A distillation framework trains deep spiking networks for flexible inference across timestep choices without separate retraining.

paragraphs: Flow of Reasoning targets the ability to produce several valid solutions to a problem. The paper argues that improving reasoning accuracy alone leaves this diversity underdeveloped: supervised fine-tuning can require large labeled datasets, while reward-maximizing reinforcement learning can concentrate on the highest-reward solutions. FoR aims to improve both solution quality and variety with limited training examples.

The method represents multistep reasoning as flow through a directed graph without cycles. It adapts GFlowNet techniques so that different reasoning paths are sampled with probabilities proportional to their rewards. This makes diversity part of the training formulation while still favoring useful solutions, rather than treating every possible reasoning path as equally desirable.

Experiments cover six tasks spanning embodied, mathematical, spatial, abstraction, and logical reasoning. With limited data, including settings using 15 examples, FoR discovers diverse, creative, high-quality solutions and substantially outperforms a broad range of inference and training methods. These results support training for a distribution of valuable reasoning paths when discovering multiple solutions matters.
icml-2025-flow-of-reasoning-training-llm.tldr: FoR adapts GFlowNet training to help language models discover diverse, high-quality reasoning paths from very few examples.

paragraphs: Process reward models evaluate individual reasoning steps, but collecting labels for every step is expensive. This paper shows theoretically and empirically that an implicit process reward model can instead emerge from training on response-level labels. The result assumes that the outcome reward is parameterized as a scaled log-likelihood ratio between a policy model and a reference model.

Under that parameterization, the approach works across different training objectives without additional process-label training cost. On MATH, the implicit model outperforms a strong Math-Shepherd-style, search-based baseline using less than one thirty-eighth of its training data. Majority voting improves performance further. Increasing both instructions and responses helps, with additional responses producing the larger gain.

The cross-entropy version is particularly data-efficient and still improves generation models with only one response per instruction. The experiments also find that instructions should match downstream tasks, response diversity brings no gains, and adding Math-Shepherd step labels produces no further improvement. These findings identify conditions under which cheaper outcome supervision can supply useful stepwise feedback.
icml-2025-free-process-rewards-without-p.tldr: With a specific likelihood-ratio reward parameterization, response-level training yields useful implicit process rewards without step-level labels.

paragraphs: Selecting good training data can improve language-model training efficiency, but a fixed selection rule does not account for how a model changes as it learns. This paper focuses on a related question: once examples have been selected, how much influence should each have at the current stage of training?

The proposed Data Weighting Model adjusts the weights of selected examples within each batch. A bi-level optimization framework updates the weighting model to reflect the trained model's changing data preferences. This makes data utilization responsive to training progress, rather than assigning the same importance to an example throughout the entire learning process.

Experiments show that the weighting model improves performance when the underlying training data are randomly selected. The learned weighting model also transfers to other selection methods and models of different sizes, indicating that it can complement existing data-selection pipelines. The authors additionally analyze how preferences evolve during training. Together, these results support treating example usefulness as something that changes with the model.
icml-2025-llm-data-selection-and-utiliza.tldr: A dynamically trained weighting model improves how LLMs use selected data as their preferences change during training.

paragraphs: MindCustomer explores image generation that combines image context with visual brain signals. The challenge is to interpret signals across people while preserving information from different input types. Those inputs can express conflicting meanings, so simply bringing them together does not ensure a coherent generated image.

The method introduces an Image-Brain Translator that generates brain responses from visual images. This supports shared neural data augmentation for more stable brain representations across subjects. The translator also maps image context into the brain representation during fusion, reducing the mismatch between the two kinds of information. A diffusion-based pipeline then integrates their distinct semantics without requiring masks and addresses conflicts to preserve context.

The authors report high-quality, natural outputs in cross-subject generation and strong generalization to new subjects with few-shot learning. These findings suggest potential for practical customization using brain signals alongside other visual context. The work is presented as an initial exploration of this combination, providing a foundation for further brain-controlled generative technologies.
icml-2025-mindcustomer-multi-context-ima.tldr: MindCustomer combines visual brain signals and image context through shared representations and diffusion-based fusion for customized image generation.

paragraphs: Unlearnable examples modify data to hinder unauthorized model training. Most existing approaches target a single task, leaving a gap for data used to train models on several tasks simultaneously. MTL-UE addresses this gap with a unified framework for generating unlearnable examples for multi-task data and models.

The framework generates perturbations with a shared generator instead of optimizing them separately for every sample. It incorporates label priors and class-specific feature embeddings to improve attack performance. Regularization within and across tasks encourages greater separation between classes while reducing variation within each class, strengthening the attack's robustness. The framework also supports dense prediction tasks and can incorporate existing surrogate-dependent unlearnable methods with limited adaptation.

Experiments report consistently superior attack performance across four multi-task datasets, three base unlearnable-example methods, five model backbones, and five task-weighting strategies. This breadth matters because multi-task training can vary in both architecture and how it balances objectives. The findings support designing data-protection perturbations around shared multi-task structure rather than treating each task in isolation.
icml-2025-mtl-ue-learning-to-learn-nothi.tldr: MTL-UE generates perturbations that hinder multi-task model training using label information and regularized class embeddings.

paragraphs: Physical adversarial attacks can disrupt face-recognition systems, but existing approaches often face tradeoffs involving visibility, effectiveness, and robustness. UVHat investigates an attack using ultraviolet emitters mounted on a hat. The paper targets black-box settings and aims to produce an invisible physical intervention that remains effective from multiple viewing angles.

Its modeling approach uses video interpolation to simulate ultraviolet light sources and represents their positions on a curved surface corresponding to the human head. This explicitly incorporates the surface geometry into adversarial face generation. A reinforcement-learning optimization strategy searches a broad space of physical and viewing parameters to improve attack performance.

The reported experiments show substantially improved attack success in black-box settings, together with stronger robustness and effectiveness across multiple angles. These findings address several weaknesses identified in earlier physical attacks within the paper's evaluation. The contribution is a combination of physical modeling and optimization that demonstrates another way face-recognition systems can be vulnerable under varied viewing conditions.
icml-2025-omni-angle-assault-an-invisibl.tldr: UVHat combines ultraviolet emitters, curved-surface modeling, and reinforcement learning to improve black-box physical attacks on face recognition across viewing angles.

paragraphs: Multi-kernel clustering combines different descriptions of similarity to capture varied patterns in data. This paper asks how vulnerable these methods are to deliberately introduced, imperceptible perturbations. It studies the problem in a black-box setting and introduces AdvMKC, a reinforcement-learning attack framework designed to mislead the resulting clusters.

A central difficulty is that clustering results can be unstable during optimization. AdvMKC uses proximal policy optimization with an advantage function to address this instability. It also separates perturbation generation from an approximation of the clustering method: a generator creates adversarial changes, while a clusterer models the target's behavior. This arrangement significantly reduces computational overhead.

The authors provide theoretical insights into how perturbations affect multi-kernel clustering and test the framework on seven datasets and eleven clustering methods, including seven traditional and four robust approaches. The evaluations report effective, robust, and transferable attacks. These findings extend adversarial assessment to a clustering setting where robustness had received comparatively little study and show the value of testing methods designed to be robust.
icml-2025-on-the-adversarial-robustness-.tldr: AdvMKC uses reinforcement learning and an approximate clusterer to evaluate multi-kernel clustering vulnerabilities through efficient black-box attacks.

paragraphs: Batched linear bandits model decision problems where feedback can influence choices only between batches. This limits how often an algorithm can adapt while learning which actions are best. Existing approaches can have strong theoretical regret guarantees yet be computationally costly or perform poorly in practice. BLAE is designed to address both sides of that gap.

The algorithm combines arm elimination, which removes less promising actions, with regularized G-optimal design for organizing exploration. It achieves minimax-optimal regret up to logarithmic factors in the time horizon T, covering both small and large numbers of available actions. It requires only O(log log T) batches. The analysis develops techniques for batchwise optimal design and sharper concentration bounds.

Numerical evaluations show low computational overhead and stronger empirical performance than state-of-the-art methods. The theoretical and experimental claims serve complementary purposes: the regret result characterizes worst-case learning efficiency, while the evaluations demonstrate practical performance. The paper's contribution is their combination within one batched algorithm across both action-count regimes.
icml-2025-optimal-and-practical-batched-.tldr: BLAE combines near-minimax regret guarantees across action-count regimes with few batches, low overhead, and strong numerical performance.

paragraphs: Before a software agent can fix an issue, it needs to locate the relevant code. OrcaLoca focuses on this navigation problem, which remains difficult even as language-model agents improve at writing and modifying software. The paper attributes part of the difficulty to weak integration between an agent's decisions and precise code-search mechanisms.

The framework combines three components: priority-based scheduling of language-model-guided actions, decomposition of actions with relevance scoring, and context pruning that accounts for distance. Together, these mechanisms organize which actions receive attention, assess their relevance, and control the context retained during localization. The contribution is a coordinated search framework centered on identifying the code associated with an issue.

On SWE-bench Lite, OrcaLoca reaches a 65.33% function match rate, reported as a new open-source state of the art. When integrated with patch generation, it also raises an open-source framework's resolved rate by 6.33 percentage points. The latter result connects better localization to successful issue resolution, showing that the search improvement benefits the broader repair workflow.
icml-2025-orcaloca-an-llm-agent-framewor.tldr: OrcaLoca improves software issue localization through prioritized search actions, relevance scoring, and context pruning, with gains in downstream issue resolution.

paragraphs: Rejecting Instruction Preferences evaluates training prompts through the responses they elicit. Its starting assumption is that low-quality prompts tend to produce responses that are both low in quality and highly variable. This shifts attention from judging a prompt in isolation to using evidence from the model's behavior on that prompt.

RIP measures the quality of the rejected response in a preference pair and the reward difference between the chosen and rejected responses. These signals are used to filter prompts from an existing dataset or construct higher-quality synthetic datasets. The approach links prompt selection to both response quality and the contrast represented by a preference pair.

The paper reports large gains over unfiltered data across several benchmarks. For Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct, reported improvements are 9.4% on AlpacaEval2 LC Win Rate, 8.7% on Arena-Hard, and 9.9% on WildBench. For Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct, Arena-Hard rises from 67.5 to 82.9. These results support the usefulness of response-based prompt filtering under the method's stated data-quality assumption.
icml-2025-r-i-p-better-models-by-surviva.tldr: RIP filters training prompts using rejected-response quality and preference reward gaps, yielding reported gains over unfiltered datasets.

paragraphs: Complex programming tasks require more than a plausible final code sample: intermediate decisions must work together. This paper addresses the gap between supervising those decisions and judging only the final result. Learned process rewards can require costly training data and become misaligned, while outcome-only feedback can be insufficient for coordinating complex reasoning.

Outcome Refining Process Supervision, or ORPS, connects the two forms of feedback through executable verification. A tree-structured search generates alternative strategies, measures their execution behavior, and scores candidates through self-critique that combines runtime feedback with reasoning. This gives the search concrete evidence about candidate programs while preserving a structure for exploring different approaches.

Across five models and three benchmarks, the experiments report consistent gains, including 26.9% higher correctness and 42.2% improved code efficiency. The authors find that ORPS helps models escape local optima in code generation. The findings suggest that verifiable program behavior can help guide intermediate reasoning, making execution feedback useful throughout the search for a solution.
icml-2025-reasoning-through-execution-un.tldr: ORPS combines tree-structured reasoning with execution feedback and self-critique to improve generated code correctness and efficiency.

paragraphs: ResearchTown investigates whether language-model agents can simulate collaborative research communities. It simplifies a community into a graph containing researcher agents and paper data nodes, connected through collaboration relationships. This representation provides a shared structure for studying activities involving multiple researchers and bodies of work.

Its TextGNN framework treats reading papers, writing papers, and writing reviews as variations of text-based message passing through that graph. The authors also introduce ResearchBench to evaluate simulation quality. Its node-masking task asks the system to predict hidden graph content and assesses similarity, creating a scalable way to compare simulations with the information being reconstructed.

Experiments indicate realistic simulations of collaborative writing and reviewing, with robust behavior across multiple researchers and diverse papers. ResearchTown also generates interdisciplinary ideas that could inspire new research directions. That potential is distinct from demonstrating a scientific discovery: the stated result concerns useful idea generation. The work combines a community representation, a unified activity model, and an evaluation benchmark for studying this possibility.
icml-2025-researchtown-simulator-of-huma.tldr: ResearchTown simulates collaborative research through language-model agents and text-based graph message passing, including potentially useful interdisciplinary idea generation.

paragraphs: Temporal point processes model event streams through an intensity function describing event occurrence over time. Simple statistical models and expressive neural models offer different strengths. Residual TPP combines them by identifying which events a statistical model explains poorly and using a neural model to handle those remaining events.

The key component is Residual Events Decomposition, or RED. It defines a weighting function that measures how well an intensity function captures event characteristics. Events with poor fit are treated as residual events. RED is designed as a flexible module that can be incorporated into any temporal point process model across a range of tasks.

In the proposed combination, a Hawkes process captures self-excitation in the data and helps identify residual events, while a neural temporal point process handles those residuals. Experiments across multiple domains report state-of-the-art goodness of fit and prediction performance, along with substantial computational advantages. The results support dividing the modeling work according to where a simpler model needs additional expressive capacity.
icml-2025-residual-tpp-a-unified-lightwe.tldr: Residual TPP combines a Hawkes process with a neural event model by identifying and modeling events the simpler component fits poorly.

paragraphs: Long reasoning chains can help language models solve mathematics problems, but they can also spend excessive effort on easy questions. This paper addresses that mismatch by training models to account for inference budgets. The objective is to allocate more computation to harder queries while recognizing that longer reasoning is not equally valuable for every problem.

Inference Budget-Constrained Policy Optimization, or IBPO, formulates this allocation as utility maximization subject to an inference budget. Models fine-tuned with the method learn to adjust their computational effort according to query difficulty. Budget awareness is therefore built into the optimization objective rather than left solely to a fixed reasoning procedure.

On MATH500, the best reported models improve over LLaMA3.1 8B Instruct by 4.14 and 5.74 percentage points using 2.16 and 4.32 times the inference budget, respectively. These correspond to relative gains of 8.08% and 11.2%. The improvements are approximately twice those of self-consistency at the same budgets, supporting learned allocation as a useful way to spend additional inference computation.
icml-2025-think-smarter-not-harder-adapt.tldr: IBPO trains language models to allocate inference effort by question difficulty, improving mathematical reasoning under specified computation budgets.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks represent information through spikes over time, creating opportunities for energy-efficient computation. Making good use of temporal features while keeping energy consumption low remains difficult. TS-SNN introduces a lightweight temporal shift module intended to improve the information available within each timestep without adding substantial computational cost.

The module shifts spike features so that past, present, and future features are integrated within a single timestep. A residual combination preserves the original features alongside the shifted ones to prevent information loss. The module adds only one learnable parameter and is designed to fit into existing architectures with minimal additional computation.

The paper reports state-of-the-art performance with fewer timesteps on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, achieving 96.72%, 80.28%, and 70.61%, respectively, while maintaining low energy consumption. These findings connect a small architectural change to improved temporal feature use. The contribution is a simple mechanism for bringing information across time into the network's processing while retaining the efficiency goals that motivate spiking architectures.
icml-2025-ts-snn-temporal-shift-module-f.tldr: TS-SNN shifts and combines spike features across time to improve accuracy with fewer timesteps and little added computation.

paragraphs: Adapting text-to-image diffusion models for very high resolutions can demand substantial data and computation. URAE develops guidelines for doing this efficiently, examining both which training data to use and which model parameters to update. Its recommendations depend on the available data and the type of model being adapted.

For data efficiency, the authors provide theoretical and empirical evidence that synthetic examples from some teacher models substantially improve convergence. When synthetic data are unavailable, tuning small components of weight matrices outperforms widely used low-rank adapters while remaining efficient. For models using guidance distillation, such as FLUX, setting the guidance scale to 1 during adaptation is crucial for satisfactory performance.

Experiments show comparable 2K-generation performance to closed-source systems such as FLUX1.1 [Pro] Ultra using 3,000 samples and 2,000 iterations, alongside new benchmarks for 4K generation. The findings make adaptation choices central to high-resolution performance: teacher data, parameter updates, and guidance settings each contribute, with their usefulness tied to the conditions studied.
icml-2025-ultra-resolution-adaptation-wi.tldr: URAE identifies data, parameter-tuning, and guidance choices that enable efficient adaptation of diffusion models for 2K and 4K image generation.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning allows clients with different data distributions to combine shared knowledge with models tailored to their own needs. This paper considers learning global and local models simultaneously. Training locally requires no communication, while collaboration can improve statistical accuracy, creating a tradeoff between information exchange and estimation quality.

The authors quantitatively characterize how the degree of personalization affects that tradeoff. Their analysis connects personalization to sample and algorithmic efficiency and offers theoretical guidance for choosing how much to personalize. This matters because personalization is not only a modeling preference; it also changes the balance between the benefits of collaboration and the resources required to obtain them.

The paper additionally establishes minimax-optimal statistical accuracy for a widely studied personalized federated learning formulation. This characterizes its performance against the best achievable worst-case accuracy. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets validate the theoretical result, and the authors verify generalizability in a non-convex setting. Together, the findings provide a quantitative basis for reasoning about personalization choices.
icml-2025-understanding-the-statistical-.tldr: The paper quantifies how personalization changes the accuracy–communication tradeoff and establishes minimax statistical guarantees for a federated learning formulation.

paragraphs: Molecular dynamics simulations help explain how atoms move and interact, but classical methods face a tradeoff between accuracy and efficiency. Many learned alternatives focus on a single molecular domain, limiting their transfer to unfamiliar systems. UniSim aims to share knowledge across domains while learning molecular changes over longer timesteps.

The method first uses multi-head pretraining on diverse molecular data to build a unified representation of atoms. It then learns long-timestep transitions from molecular dynamics trajectories through a stochastic interpolant framework. A force-guidance module supports rapid adaptation to different chemical environments, connecting the shared representation to the dynamics of a particular system.

Experiments report highly competitive performance across small molecules, peptides, and proteins. This range is central to the contribution: the model is designed to reuse knowledge across molecular categories instead of remaining confined to a single domain. The findings support combining broad atomic pretraining, learned long-step transitions, and force guidance as a unified approach to simulating biomolecular dynamics.
icml-2025-unisim-a-unified-simulator-for.tldr: UniSim combines shared atomic representations, learned long-timestep transitions, and force guidance to simulate dynamics across molecular domains.
